Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning

 

Annan Zhang 1  Shengjie Song 1  Wenshuai Yao 1  Tianmiao 2  Lihao Zhang 1 

††footnotetext: 1Peking University 2Beihang University. Correspondence to: Annan Zhang <annan@pku.edu.cn>.
Preliminary work. Under review by the Machine Learning and Systems (MLSys) Conference. Do not distribute.
Abstract

Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record’s clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record’s activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA–Opacus witness reaches 15.0×15.0\times the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record–layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches 1.065​C1.065C while every control stays within CC, and forcing one layer’s outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields ε\varepsilon lower bounds (3.253.25 at δ=10−5\delta=10^{-5}) below the advertised guarantee (4.384.38). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.

1 Introduction

Fine-tuning large language models on sensitive data increasingly follows one recipe: differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) (Abadi et al., 2016) trains low-rank adapters (Hu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022) on top of a frozen backbone that is quantized to fit in accelerator memory (Dettmers et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2023). Each component is mature, and off-the-shelf libraries compose them; NVIDIA NeMo Safe-Synthesizer, for example, pins bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus and Transformers together for private training (NVIDIA NeMo, 2026). The privacy accountant then certifies the composition, provided that its inputs mean what it assumes. We show that whenever such a stack batches records through LLM.int8, one of those assumptions fails.

DP-SGD clips each record’s gradient to norm CC and adds Gaussian noise calibrated to the resulting sensitivity. The argument assumes that changing one record leaves every other record’s clipped gradient unchanged. DP libraries protect this premise by rejecting layers that mix examples, such as batch normalization, and they treat the physical batch size as a pure performance knob: virtual batching splits a logical batch into memory-sized pieces without changing the privacy analysis (Yousefpour et al., 2021). Frozen quantized layers pass these checks because they own no trainable parameters. Owning no parameters, however, is not the same as computing each record independently.

LLM.int8 (Dettmers et al., 2022) makes the gap concrete. It quantizes activations row by row, except for outlier feature columns, which it computes in FP16. Writing Ar,t,:A_{r,t,:} for token row tt of record rr, the outlier set of a batch DD is

O(D)={j:∃r∈D,t:|Ar,t,j|≥τ}.O(D)=\{\,j:\ \exists\,r\in D,\,t:\ |A_{r,t,j}|\geq\tau\,\}. (1)

Because the union ranges over all records, adding one record can move a column of every other record from the INT8 path to the FP16 path and change their outputs and adapter gradients, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row (Figure 1). Unlike leakage through shared quantization scales (Foerster et al., 2026), no numerical statistic is pooled across the batch; what is shared is the decision of which precision path each column takes.

This paper asks three questions. How much can such routing coupling inflate the sensitivity of the clipped sum, and which implementation contract rules it out? Does the native stack actually exhibit the coupling, on constructed and on natural inputs? And does the inflation reach the released model? We make the following contributions.

  • •

    Analysis and contract (§3–4). An influence bound shows that mm altered unchanged contributions raise add/remove sensitivity from CC to (2​m+1)​C(2m{+}1)C, a limit our constructed witness attains. A record-isolation contract restores the separable bound, and record-owned precision dispatch satisfies it with the same INT8 and FP16 GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, changing only the masks.

  • •

    A native audit (§5). We audit the pinned CUDA stack along an evidence ladder (operator, LoRA–Opacus composition, pretrained OPT-125M), validate every per-record gradient against independent autograd, trace native kernel dispatch, and pair each measurement with four controls: record isolation, threshold zero, BF16 and NF4.

  • •

    Findings (§6). (i) The constructed composition reaches 14.998​C14.998C, essentially the worst case, while all controls stay within CC. (ii) On natural text, other records alter 5–20% of OPT-125M’s record–layer precision splits as the physical batch grows from 2 to 16. (iii) Once every gradient is clipped, 10 of 64 candidate neighbors exceed the bound by 1.4–6.5% in an exploratory analysis, and the top pair reaches 1.0653​C1.0653C in 40 fresh native cases in which every control stays within CC. (iv) The excess traces to one column added to one layer’s union; forcing that mask removes it. (v) A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields ε\varepsilon lower bounds below the advertised guarantee; a power analysis shows that resolving the measured excess at the release level would take about 200 times more draws.

Scope.

Our target is the proof’s premise: the sensitivity contract fails natively, while the release-level audit detects no violation of the advertised guarantee. The lesson is general: a DP-SGD proof certifies a computation, not module labels. Physical batching and data-dependent numerics are part of the privacy mechanism, so they must be made record-owned or be audited. Simple configurations (singleton physical batches, threshold zero, weight-only NF4, or BF16) restored the bound in every setting we measured.

2 Background

Privacy unit and the audited sum.

A record owns all of its token rows, its padding and attention-mask convention, its loss terms and any private randomness. Neighboring datasets differ by adding or removing one record (our primary relation) or by replacing one. At step tt we condition on a fixed transcript HtH_{t} of public state and previously released private outputs; persistent private state that was never released, such as a cached routing decision, is not public. The contribution that DP-SGD actually clips is

hr​(D,Ht)=gr​(D,Ht)​min⁡{1,C/‖gr​(D,Ht)‖2},h_{r}(D;H_{t})=g_{r}(D;H_{t})\,\min\{1,\,C/\|g_{r}(D;H_{t})\|_{2}\}, (2)

where gr​(D,Ht)g_{r}(D;H_{t}) is record rr’s adapter gradient as computed inside batch DD, with the zero-gradient case defined by continuity. The first audited object is the clipped sum

F⁡(D)=∑r∈Dhr​(D,Ht),F(D)=\textstyle\sum_{r\in D}h_{r}(D;H_{t}), (3)

to which DP-SGD adds 𝒩⁡(0,σ2​C2​I)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}C^{2}I) before averaging and the optimizer step. If each hrh_{r} depends only on record rr, then ‖F⁡(D)−F⁡(D′)‖2≤C\|F(D)-F(D^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq C for add/remove neighbors and ≤2​C\leq 2C for replacement: the separable bound. A per-example interface such as Opacus’s grad_sample reports grg_{r}, but it does not show that grg_{r} depends only on rr. We use full sampling (q=1q{=}1) and a fixed public loss divisor throughout, so that sampler or normalization effects cannot masquerade as routing effects; a data-dependent divisor under add/remove adjacency would need its own analysis.

LLM.int8 mixed-precision decomposition.

For a frozen linear layer with flattened activations AA (all token rows of all records in the physical batch), LLM.int8 computes the outlier set O⁡(D)O(D) of Eq. (1) with threshold τ\tau (6 by default). Each row’s quantization scale is its absolute maximum over entries below τ\tau, a purely row-local statistic. The columns in O⁡(D)O(D) are then zeroed in every row’s INT8 codes and recomputed in FP16, and the two partial products are added (Dettmers et al., 2022). A record’s output therefore depends on other records only through O⁡(D)O(D), which decides, for every row, which columns take which precision path.

Threat model.

Differential privacy is a worst-case guarantee: the sensitivity bound must hold for every pair of neighboring datasets, including pairs whose differing record is chosen by an adversary who knows the model and the other records. A single measured pair whose clipped sums are farther apart than the separable bound therefore refutes that bound for the computation and lower-bounds its true sensitivity, whereas a natural pair that stays within the bound says nothing about the worst case. LLM.int8 hands such an adversary a direct lever: a record with a large activation in a column that no other record triggers moves that column to FP16 for every co-batched record. Our constructed witness (§6.1) shows that this lever can push the clipped sum to the limit of Proposition 1. We do not search for adversarial natural-text records.

3 Cross-Record Influence

3.1 How much can influence inflate sensitivity?

Proposition 1 (Influence bound).

For replacement neighbors of equal size, suppose at most mm unchanged contributions hrh_{r} differ between DD and D′D^{\prime}. Then

‖F⁡(D)−F⁡(D′)‖2≤2​(m+1)​C.\|F(D)-F(D^{\prime})\|_{2}\leq 2(m+1)C. (4)

For add/remove neighbors, if at most mm common contributions differ, the bound is (2​m+1)​C(2m+1)C.

Proof.

Each changed common contribution moves by at most 2​C2C by the triangle inequality. Replacement adds one more pair of clipped contributions, also bounded by 2​C2C; add/remove adds one unmatched vector of norm at most CC. Summing gives the bounds. ∎

Proposition 1 is elementary, and it exposes a missing premise rather than a new privacy theorem. A changed routing mask may leave gradients unchanged, changed gradients may cancel, and a pair’s distance may stay below the separable bound. Conversely, a measured distance above the separable bound is a sensitivity witness: it shows that the standard proof does not apply to that computation. The bound is tight; our constructed composition attains (2​m+1)​C(2m{+}1)C for m=7m{=}7 (§6.1). A witness alone does not refute an advertised guarantee, which concerns the released output.

3.2 From a sensitivity witness to the released output

For the declared real-valued one-step mechanism M⁡(D)=F⁡(D)+ZM(D)=F(D)+Z with Z∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​C2​I)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}C^{2}I), fix a neighboring pair, let Δ=‖F⁡(D)−F⁡(D′)‖2\Delta=\|F(D)-F(D^{\prime})\|_{2} and μ=Δ/(σ​C)\mu=\Delta/(\sigma C). Projecting the Gaussian likelihood ratio onto the mean difference gives the exact hockey-stick divergence (Balle and Wang, 2018)

δpair​(ε)=Φ⁡(μ2−εμ)−eε​Φ​(−μ2−εμ),\delta_{\rm pair}(\varepsilon)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu}{2}-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}\right)-e^{\varepsilon}\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac{\mu}{2}-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}\right), (5)

which is zero for Δ=0\Delta{=}0. If δpair\delta_{\rm pair} exceeds the advertised δ\delta at the advertised ε\varepsilon, the pair refutes the guarantee for this mechanism. A modest excess changes ε\varepsilon modestly: μ=1.065\mu{=}1.065 instead of 11 raises the one-step ε\varepsilon at δ=10−5\delta{=}10^{-5} from 4.384.38 to 4.714.71 (§6.5). The test transfers to the released adapter when the output is a known invertible affine map of the noisy gradient, as for one SGD step from a fixed initialization; general optimizers or later training may lose information, and finite-precision noise is a different mechanism that must be audited rather than assumed to follow Eq. (5) (Mironov, 2012).

4 Record-Owned Precision Dispatch

4.1 The isolation contract

Proposition 2 (Compositional record isolation).

Condition on HtH_{t}. Suppose that every forward and backward operation producing record rr’s adapter contribution reads only rr’s data, public state and rr’s assigned randomness; that routing decisions and persistent scratch state obey the same rule; and that numerical choices affecting the result do not depend on other records. Then each contribution is record-isolated, and Eq. (3) has sensitivity at most CC for add/remove and 2​C2C for replacement neighbors.

Proof.

Topologically order the forward graph and the reverse-mode computations. Every record-owned input of a common record is unchanged. Each subsequent operation has unchanged admissible inputs and numerical choices, so its output is unchanged; the same induction covers backward intermediates and the final contribution. Clipping is record-local, so Proposition 1 with m=0m{=}0 gives the bounds. For randomized local computation the argument holds under a fixed record-owned random tape, and a bound that holds for every tape survives averaging over tapes. ∎

The contract is sufficient, not necessary: a coupled program could admit a different valid sensitivity argument. It also does not follow that a standard GEMM backend satisfies the numerical-invariance condition, since grouping can change reductions, tile selection or backward kernels. Bitwise agreement with isolated execution is therefore a separate implementation target; if it fails, the implementation must constrain the backend or declare a different record-local numerical reference. Small numerical differences are not a noninterference proof.

4.2 Record-owned routing semantics

Define each record’s own outlier set Or={j:∃t,|Ar,t,j|≥τ}O_{r}=\{j:\exists t,\ |A_{r,t,j}|\geq\tau\}. The reference semantics executes LLM.int8 on all tokens of one record at a time (token-local routing is another valid choice, with a different numerical reference). A batched implementation masks each row with its owner’s OrO_{r}, evaluates one dense integer product, and adds only that record’s correction:

Yr,t=Q¬Or(Ar,t)Q(W)⊤+Ar,t,OrW:,Or⊤.Y_{r,t}=Q_{\neg O_{r}}(A_{r,t})\,Q(W)^{\top}+A_{r,t,O_{r}}\,W_{:,O_{r}}^{\top}. (6)

Here Q¬OrQ_{\neg O_{r}} includes the reference scaling and dequantization; Eq. (6) specifies ownership, not a fused instruction sequence. Because frozen weights are public, the union of weight columns W:,∪rOrW_{:,\cup_{r}O_{r}} may be fetched once per batch; the union must never decide which correction another record receives. Shared allocation, scheduling and caching are admissible only when they change no record’s arithmetic, random stream or later private state.

Implementation.

Algorithm 1 realizes Eq. (6) with LLM.int8’s own kernels. It needs only record offsets, which the adapter receives before flattening: a segmented reduction turns the per-entry threshold test into per-record sets OrO_{r}, and per-row masks replace the per-column mask. A grouped kernel can additionally skip the zeros in RR by issuing per-record or sparse residual products while preserving row order. The backward pass needs the same ownership audit for input-gradient products, adapter activations, clipping buffers and dropout masks: frozen layers pass data-dependent activations to trainable modules, so validating only directly trainable parameters, as Opacus does, cannot establish Proposition 2. Shared outlier caches must be record-scoped or cleared unless their privacy cost is accounted for.

Cost.

Algorithm 1 issues the same INT8 and FP16 GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, and building the sets OrO_{r} reuses the threshold comparisons that LLM.int8 already performs. Ownership does not add FP16 work either: each row multiplies only its own outlier columns, so a grouped kernel that skips the zeros in RR does 1.5–7.5% less correction work than batched LLM.int8 on our OPT-125M traces at B=2B{=}2–1616 (weighted by layer width; Figure 2a shows the unweighted share). In those traces the correction covers at most 8 of a layer’s 768 or 3,072 input columns. Record ownership is therefore arithmetic-neutral by construction; the remaining engineering lies in mask construction, kernel design and numerical invariance, a clear target for an optimized kernel.

Simpler alternatives.

The same contract is met by singleton physical batches, threshold zero (no outlier path), a public calibrated outlier mask (Ashkboos et al., 2023), per-vector sparse outliers (Hooper et al., 2024), weight-only NF4 (Dettmers et al., 2023), or an unquantized BF16 backbone. A grouped kernel is worthwhile only if it improves the resulting quality/resource frontier; native batched execution can enter an equal-privacy comparison only with a valid worst-case influence bound, never with a sampled maximum treated as global.

5 Audit Methodology

Stack.

All experiments run on one NVIDIA H100 NVL with PyTorch 2.8.0+cu126, bitsandbytes 0.49.1 (bitsandbytes Contributors, 2026), PEFT 0.18.1 (Hugging Face, 2026a), Opacus 1.5.4 (Opacus Contributors, 2026) and Transformers 5.12.0 (Hugging Face, 2026b), the versions pinned by Safe-Synthesizer commit 7f3b767c (NVIDIA NeMo, 2026); the operator experiment uses bitsandbytes 0.48.1. We execute the pinned components, not Safe-Synthesizer’s entry point.

Procedure.

Algorithm 2 summarizes the audit we apply to the pretrained model: a native screen, an exploratory re-clipping analysis, native validation of the top pair, causal localization, and a release audit. The rest of this section details its arms, checks and measurements.

Arms.

Each experiment compares native batched execution with matched controls on identical inputs and, for adapters, identical canonical FP32 initializations: native batched INT8 (LLM.int8, τ=6\tau{=}6, all records in one physical batch); record-isolated INT8 (one record per physical forward, accumulated with Opacus virtual batching into a single logical noise/update step, never eight separately noised steps); threshold zero (no outlier path); a BF16 backbone; and NF4 weight-only quantization. The four controls remove the batch-wide union in four different ways.

Validation.

Wherever applicable, every case checks that (i) Opacus grad_sample equals independent per-record autograd of the same realized batch loss, its sum equals the batch backward, and every trainable coordinate is covered; (ii) each INT8 forward calls the loaded library’s cint8_vector_quant, cigemmlt_32 and cdequant_mm_int32_fp16 entry points, and backward does not re-run quantization; (iii) clipping matches Opacus’s formula, including its 10−610^{-6} stabilizer; and (iv) identical-batch repeats give exactly zero distance, so the measurement floor is zero. These checks separate a validated native computation from a sensitivity calculation on an emulator.

Measurement.

We compute Δ=‖F⁡(D)−F⁡(D′)‖2\Delta=\|F(D)-F(D^{\prime})\|_{2} in FP64 from the saved FP32 contributions and report the ratio κ=Δ/C\kappa=\Delta/C for add/remove and Δ/(2​C)\Delta/(2C) for replacement. Losses are summed with a fixed public divisor, q=1q{=}1, and the noise multiplier is 1. Each case also executes one logical Opacus noise, accountant and SGD step, which verifies the release path but cannot estimate a release distribution (§6.5). For OPT-125M, exceedance is declared only above the bound plus an absolute margin of 10−410^{-4} (plus ten times the repeat distance, which is zero), fixed in the protocol before the screen. All attempts are retained, including failed ones (Appendix B).

6 Results

Every sensitivity rung of the evidence ladder shows the same pattern: native batching breaks the separable bound and every control stays within it. Table 1 summarizes the ladder, from a constructed 15×15\times excess to a single column in one layer of pretrained OPT-125M; the subsections follow the same order.

6.1 Constructed witnesses

We first ask whether the native kernels execute the coupling at all, using a construction whose effect is easy to read (details in Appendix A). Eight records each contribute one activation row to a frozen INT8 layer with weight [1,0][1,0]; two exact zeros pad the inner dimension to K=4K{=}4, avoiding a narrow-KK floating-point fallback. An FP32 scalar bias is the only trainable parameter, τ=6\tau{=}6, and C=0.005C{=}0.005. The seven unchanged rows are [1.234,5][1.234,5]; the eighth changes from [1,5][1,5] to [6.1,5][6.1,5] and crosses τ\tau in column 0. Row scales stay at 5, but column 0 joins the union, so the unchanged rows’ first entry moves from the INT8 path (output 1.2207031251.220703125) to FP16 (1.2343751.234375). Their common label is the midpoint of these two native outputs, fixed by a pilot, so each bias gradient flips sign (∓0.0068359375\mp 0.0068359375) and each clipped contribution moves by 2​C2C. This loss geometry is chosen to make the effect legible; it is not a frequency estimate.

Operator.

The trace records the actual CUDA quantization codes, row scales, outlier indices and per-record bias derivatives. The outlier set changes from empty to {0}\{0\}, and the replacement distance is exactly 14​Cf14C_{f}, where CfC_{f} is the FP32 representation of CC: seven times the separable bound (Table 2). A NumPy reference of the same arithmetic gives identical outputs. Record isolation, threshold zero, BF16 and an identical-input null all give zero distance.

Library composition.

We replace the bias with an actual rank-one PEFT LoRA adapter (four trainable entries in AA, one in BB; at the B=0B{=}0 initialization only BB’s gradient is nonzero) and run Opacus per-record gradients, clipping, noise and SGD on the pinned 0.49.1 stack. Adding the eighth record changes the union from empty to {0}\{0\} and reverses all seven common records’ LoRA gradients. The add/remove distance is 14.998​C14.998C, within 0.02%0.02\% of the (2​m+1)​C=15​C(2m{+}1)C=15C worst case of Proposition 1; replacement gives 6.999×2​C6.999\times 2C. Every control stays within its separable bound: add/remove distances equal the added record’s own contribution (0.99999979​C0.99999979C), and replacement distances are zero. In all 20 measurements (5 arms ×\times 4 inputs) Opacus grad_sample matched independent autograd on the same realized batch. Under the declared real-valued Gaussian mechanism (Eq. (5)), a pair this far apart would raise the one-step ε\varepsilon at δ=10−5\delta{=}10^{-5} and σ=1\sigma{=}1 from 4.38 to about 176; we did not audit the finite-precision release of this constructed pair.

6.2 Coupling is routine on natural text

Does the pathway carry traffic on natural inputs? We instrument pretrained OPT-125M (Zhang et al., 2022) with native LLM.int8 (τ=6\tau{=}6) and rank-8 LoRA adapters on the query and value projections (294,912 trainable parameters in 48 tensors), on the first 16 TinyStories training windows (Eldan and Li, 2023) (256 tokens each, official padding masks, dropout off, masked next-token loss with fixed public divisor 255). At physical batch sizes 2, 4, 8 and 16, every configuration passes Opacus validation and executes a real clipping, noise and optimizer step with complete per-record gradients. Each step issues 72 native INT8 quantization, integer-GEMM and dequantization calls; 42 of the 72 layers have a nonempty outlier union, which matches the union recomputed from the B×256B{\times}256 activation rows exactly.

For every layer we also record each record’s own set OrO_{r}. Figure 2a shows how often it differs from the union. At B=2B{=}2, 4.8% of (record, layer) pairs in the 42 outlier-carrying layers compute some column in FP16 only because another record crossed τ\tau; at B=16B{=}16 the share is 20.1%, and 7.0% of all FP16 columns applied to a record were triggered by others. Figure 2b shows where this happens at B=16B{=}16: every record is coupled in layer 7’s attention input, as are 13 and 14 records in layer 9’s attention input and layer 11’s first feed-forward projection, while 15 of the 22 outlier-carrying cells show no coupling at all. Most outlier columns are shared by every record, consistent with the systematic outlier features documented by Dettmers et al. (2022). Only 3–7 columns per batch are owned by a single record, and only those can leave the union when one record is removed. Whether such a change moves a clipped gradient is the question of the next experiment.

6.3 Sensitivity on pretrained OPT-125M

We fix a seven-record baseline DD (TinyStories rows 16–22) and consider adding each of 64 candidate records (rows 24–87), keeping every outcome. The initial screen at C=1C{=}1 is negative: over the 64 candidates, the largest native add/remove distance is 0.99999921​C0.99999921C.

Why the screen missed.

Re-clipping the saved native per-record gradients at nine radii (Figure 3a; 576 exploratory scores, none discarded) explains the negative result. At C=1C{=}1 most per-record gradients are shorter than CC, so the added record contributes less than CC and absorbs the cross-record change. Once every gradient is clipped (C≤0.25C\leq 0.25), κ\kappa no longer depends on CC, and 10 of the 64 candidates exceed the bound by 1.4–6.5%. Small radii at which most gradients are clipped are common in private language-model fine-tuning (Li et al., 2022), so this regime is practically relevant.

Native validation.

We then froze the top-ranked candidate (row 75) and ran 40 fresh native cases: the baseline, an earlier addition (row 23), the selected addition and an identical repeat, under native batching and all four controls, at C=0.001C{=}0.001 (the top-ranked radius) and C=0.25C{=}0.25. All 40 cases pass the execution, initialization, derivative and clipping checks. Native batching gives Δ=0.2663144763=1.065257905​C\Delta=0.2663144763=1.065257905C at C=0.25C{=}0.25, above the bound plus the protocol margin. At C=0.001C{=}0.001 it gives the same ratio, 1.0652579041.065257904, but the absolute excess (6.5×10−56.5\times 10^{-5}) is below the 10−410^{-4} margin; since κ\kappa is scale-free in this regime the two runs measure the same relative excess, and we report the margin outcome as declared. The excess is four orders of magnitude larger than any control’s deviation from CC (at most 2.4×10−62.4\times 10^{-6} for isolation, threshold zero and BF16, and 4.7×10−44.7\times 10^{-4} below CC for NF4; Figure 3b). All replacement ratios, including the native 0.6710.671, stay below 2​C2C. Because sensitivity is a supremum over neighboring datasets, this one pair already shows that the native computation’s add/remove sensitivity is at least 1.0653​C1.0653C, not CC. Selection and validation belong to one discovery study on one baseline batch, so these results show that the separable premise fails for a natural pretrained configuration; they do not estimate how often it fails across batches or models.

6.4 One layer’s mask causes the excess

Across all 72 INT8 layers, exactly one union differs between DD and D′D^{\prime} (Figure 4a): in decoder layer 6’s first feed-forward projection, adding row 75 grows the union from {422}\{422\} to {422,706}\{422,706\}. The seven common records’ LoRA gradients differ by 0.048–0.071 in ℓ2\ell_{2} norm.

Forward factorial.

We capture the common records’ input activations at that layer under DD and D′D^{\prime} and cross the two value tensors with the two masks, with the input batch fixed to DD, the original quantization kernel and FP16 correction, and the other 71 layers unmodified; an intervention is rejected if its forced union would omit a natural outlier. All seven forwards (two native references, an identical repeat and four factorial cells) complete. Reference losses and all 72 masks match the parent experiment bitwise, and both diagonal cells reproduce their native logits bitwise. The captured activations are bitwise identical under DD and D′D^{\prime}, so changing only the values has no effect, whereas changing only the mask reproduces the entire common-record logit change (maximum absolute difference 0.366300.36630, ℓ2\ell_{2} difference 309.3763309.3763; Figure 4b).

Backward intervention.

Four further native Opacus cases force that layer to use the frozen union O⁡(D′)O(D^{\prime}) in both batches, keeping the original inputs, autograd function and backward path; the two unforced cases reproduce all six saved parent arrays bitwise, and an independent CPU reconciliation checks every saved array. Under the forced union the clipped-sum distance falls from 1.065257905​C1.065257905C to 0.999997838​C0.999997838C, and each common record’s gradient change shrinks from 0.048–0.071 to 1.11.1–2.7×10−62.7\times 10^{-6} (Figure 4c). The residual is not zero (largest coordinate difference 1.1×10−71.1\times 10^{-7}), so exact independence is not established; we have not attributed the residual, and batch-shape-dependent kernel numerics, which Proposition 2 also excludes, are one candidate. Because the forced mask is chosen post hoc from D′D^{\prime}, the intervention localizes the cause; it is not a deployable private policy.

6.5 Does the excess reach the released model?

Sensitivity describes an intermediate sum; a privacy guarantee describes the released output. We therefore audit actual releases of the selected pair at C=0.25C{=}0.25. The audit replays the accepted deterministic clipped sums for DD and D′D^{\prime} through unmodified Opacus 1.5.4 noising and scaling and Torch SGD (learning rate 0.01, noise multiplier 1, divisor 1), resetting all 294,912 FP32 adapter coordinates before each draw. Anchors reproduce both parent noised gradients and released adapters bitwise. Forward, backward and clipping are not re-run, and noise comes from the pinned non-cryptographic CUDA generator.

Eight 250,000-draw shards give 10610^{6} releases per neighbor, two million in total, excluding qualification and warm-up draws. Each shard takes 12–13 minutes (≈\approx3 ms per release; 1.7 GPU-hours overall). The test statistic projects the released FP32 adapter displacement, in FP64, onto the clipped-sum difference direction, scaled by the learning rate times σ​C\sigma C; internal gradients are used only as diagnostics. For each δ∈{10−3,10−5,10−6}\delta\in\{10^{-3},10^{-5},10^{-6}\}, half of each neighbor’s draws select a threshold among 1,001 pooled quantiles by maximizing the empirical log-ratio objective (ties go to the lowest threshold), and the other half evaluates it with a strict inequality, without re-selection. One-sided Clopper–Pearson bounds at α=0.05/6\alpha=0.05/6 (nominal family-wise 95% over the three δ\delta) give a lower bound pLp_{L} on the D′D^{\prime} tail and an upper bound qUq_{U} on the DD tail, and

εlb=max⁡{0,log⁡((pL−δ)/qU)}.\varepsilon_{\rm lb}=\max\{0,\ \log((p_{L}-\delta)/q_{U})\}. (7)

All three δ\delta select the same threshold, 5.20835.2083. Held-out counts are 1,043/500,0001{,}043/500{,}000 for D′D^{\prime} and 23/500,00023/500{,}000 for DD, so pL=1.935×10−3p_{L}=1.935\times 10^{-3} and qU=7.456×10−5q_{U}=7.456\times 10^{-5}. The resulting bounds (2.53, 3.25 and 3.26 at δ=10−3\delta=10^{-3}, 10−510^{-5} and 10−610^{-6}) lie below the ideal real-Gaussian curves both at the advertised μ=1\mu{=}1 (3.14, 4.38, 4.89) and at the measured μ=1.065\mu{=}1.065 (3.39, 4.71, 5.25; Figure 5a). The audit detects no violation of the advertised guarantee.

How large would an audit need to be?

The audit is resolution-limited. Plugging the expected tail counts of an ideal Gaussian release into the same Clopper–Pearson procedure, even with an oracle threshold, yields only about 3.1 (μ=1\mu{=}1) and 3.3 (μ=1.065\mu{=}1.065) at δ=10−5\delta{=}10^{-5} with 5×1055\times 10^{5} held-out draws per neighbor; the observed 3.25 lies between them, so the finite-precision release is consistent with an ideal Gaussian at the measured sensitivity. Repeating the calculation for larger audits (Figure 5b), the expected bound for the measured pair first exceeds the advertised ε=4.38\varepsilon{=}4.38 at about 1.0×1081.0\times 10^{8} held-out draws per neighbor: 206 times our audit, or roughly 350 GPU-hours at our replay cost. The native sensitivity check of §6.3 exposed the same excess deterministically, in a handful of cases. For small excesses, verifying the sensitivity contract directly is far cheaper than detecting its consequence in the release. Nominal Monte Carlo coverage also assumes that the pinned generator represents the intended distribution, so the audit is not a formal finite-precision privacy proof.

7 Related Work

Private fine-tuning.

DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016) with parameter-efficient adapters is a standard route to private language-model fine-tuning (Yu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022). Opacus (Yousefpour et al., 2021) computes per-example gradients and its validator rejects known cross-example layers such as batch normalization; the JAX Privacy documentation explicitly warns about cross-example operations and recommends per-example execution where possible (JAX Privacy Contributors, 2026). Record isolation is thus an established obligation, not our invention; we show that a frozen, parameter-free quantized layer violates it in a widely used stack and measure the consequences.

Implementation-level DP failures.

Floating-point implementations can break mechanisms that are private over the reals (Mironov, 2012), DP libraries widely underestimate sensitivity because of finite-precision arithmetic (Casacuberta et al., 2022), and privacy auditing has exposed bugs in DP training code (Tramèr et al., 2022). The failure we study is of a different kind: one record’s arithmetic depends on other records through a data-dependent precision routing decision.

Privacy auditing.

Auditing DP-SGD with instantiated neighbors and Clopper–Pearson lower bounds on ε\varepsilon is standard (Jagielski et al., 2020; Nasr et al., 2021), and tight or single-run variants reduce its cost (Nasr et al., 2023; Steinke et al., 2023). We use a fixed-pair audit of actual released adapters to test whether a measured sensitivity excess reaches the output; our result shows how many draws such an audit needs before it can resolve a small excess.

Cross-example flows in batched execution.

Batch normalization couples examples and is excluded by DP libraries. Quantamination shows that dynamic quantization with shared scales leaks data across a batch (Foerster et al., 2026), and Architectural Backdoors develops within-batch data stealing together with batch noninterference checks that include dynamic quantization (Küchler et al., 2026). We build on this boundary. In LLM.int8 the scales are row-local and the coupling runs through outlier-column ownership; we measure its effect on clipped DP-SGD sensitivity and on the released update.

Quantized training and inference.

LLM.int8 (Dettmers et al., 2022) and QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) enable fine-tuning on quantized backbones. QUIK selects outlier columns by public calibration (Ashkboos et al., 2023) and KVQuant keeps sparse outliers per vector (Hooper et al., 2024); both avoid batch-dependent routing, and their optimized kernels are the baselines any grouped record-owned kernel must beat. DPQuant studies how quantization affects the utility of private training (Gao et al., 2026); it does not address the sensitivity premise studied here.

8 Discussion

Implications for system builders.

First, validate data dependence, not parameter ownership. Opacus’s validator accepts OPT-125M at every batch size we tried, although batching exceeds the bound; a batch-invariance test that compares each record’s grad_sample under native batching with singleton execution, as our isolation control does, would have flagged it. Second, treat the physical batch size as privacy-relevant unless per-record computation is shown to be batch-independent: virtual batching is privacy-neutral only under that condition, and an expected Poisson batch of one does not by itself guarantee singleton execution. Third, derive routing from public calibration or from already released state; reading the current private batch before a valid release is a different operation. Fourth, record a runtime manifest read from the executing objects (package versions, kernel dispatch, trainable flags, physical and logical batch sizes, loss normalization, clipping, sampler, accountant and noise settings), so that an auditor can check the computation the accountant certifies rather than the configuration file. Record-local configurations restored the bound in all our experiments, but they have different costs: threshold zero removes the outlier path whose absence degrades large models (Dettmers et al., 2022), singleton execution costs throughput, and BF16 costs memory.

Beyond LLM.int8.

Any decision computed over the physical batch is a candidate channel of the same kind: activation scales computed per tensor rather than per row, as in dynamically scaled FP8 or INT8 recipes (Micikevicius et al., 2022; Foerster et al., 2026); capacity-limited mixture-of-experts routing, which drops a token when its expert overflows (Fedus et al., 2022); and kernels whose reduction order depends on the batch shape. None of these needs a trainable parameter to violate Proposition 2, and each can be screened with the same batch-invariance test.

Scope and future work.

Our natural-data evidence covers one model (OPT-125M), one corpus (TinyStories) and one baseline batch, with discovery, radius selection, validation and auditing in one exploratory study; measuring prevalence is the next step. Larger OPT models, where outlier features are more pronounced (Dettmers et al., 2022), an independently pretrained lineage and a second corpus are natural targets. We analyze one step with full sampling; multi-step training under Poisson sampling and its accounting are not audited. We executed Safe-Synthesizer’s pinned components but not its entry point, whose default physical batch of one is a null case for the union. Our controls and interventions do not verify every backward dispatch, schedule or cache. Finally, record-owned dispatch is specified but not yet implemented as an optimized kernel. A fair evaluation would compare it with optimized singleton or vectorized isolation, a public calibrated mask with fused correction, per-vector sparse residuals, BF16 and NF4 at equal privacy, with the checkpoint, privacy unit, adjacency, logical batch, sampler, loss, CC, adapter rank, data order and tuning budget held fixed.

9 Conclusion

Frozen weights do not make records independent. In LLM.int8, a batch-wide outlier union lets one record set the precision of every other record’s activations, and the native bitsandbytes, PEFT and Opacus stack executes this path. A constructed composition reaches 15×15\times the DP-SGD add/remove bound, and on pretrained OPT-125M with natural text a selected neighbor exceeds it by 6.5% once clipping is active, an excess traced to one column in one layer. A two-million-draw audit finds no release-level violation; what fails is the proof’s premise. Detecting an excess this small in released outputs would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract exposes it in a few native runs. Because record-owned routing needs no extra arithmetic and simple record-local configurations restore the bound, private training stacks should enforce, or test, record ownership of data-dependent numerics instead of inferring it from frozen parameters.

Appendix A Constructed Witness Details

Operator arithmetic.

The frozen layer is a genuine bitsandbytes Linear8bitLt with frozen Int8Params and no internal bias; an external FP32 scalar bias is the only trainable parameter. The weight [1,0][1,0] and all activation rows are padded with two exact zeros to inner dimension K=4K{=}4. Each row’s scale is its absolute maximum over entries below τ=6\tau{=}6, which is 5 for every row in both batches. Without an outlier column, the unchanged entry 1.2341.234 is coded as round⁡(1.234⋅127/5)=31\mathrm{round}(1.234\cdot 127/5)=31 and dequantizes to 31⋅5/127≈1.220531\cdot 5/127\approx 1.2205, stored in FP16 as 1.2207031251.220703125. Once the replaced row’s 6.16.1 puts column 0 into the union, the same entry is zeroed in the INT8 codes and recomputed in FP16, giving 1.2343751.234375. The recorded native outputs equal these values exactly.

Labels and gradients.

A pilot obtains the two native unchanged-record outputs; their FP32 midpoint, 1.22753906251.2275390625, is then fixed as the common label of the seven unchanged records in both neighboring batches and in every control. With squared-error loss the unchanged records’ bias derivatives are −0.0068359375-0.0068359375 and +0.0068359375+0.0068359375, both larger than CC in magnitude, so each clipped contribution moves from −C-C to +C+C. The replaced record’s label is −100-100, so its clipped contribution is +C+C in both batches. The labels are common to the compared datasets but deliberately chosen; they do not represent a natural task.

Exact values.

Writing Cf=0.004999999888241291C_{f}=0.004999999888241291 for the FP32 clipping constant, the native replacement distance is Δ=14​Cf=0.06999999843537807\Delta=14C_{f}=0.06999999843537807, so Δ/(2​Cf)\Delta/(2C_{f}) is exactly 7. FP64 accumulation of the FP32 contributions is exact for this fixture, and the native FP32 sums agree, so the effect is not produced by a decimal clipping constant or a reduction discrepancy. The LoRA–Opacus composition uses summed losses with public divisor 1, q=1q{=}1, C=0.005C{=}0.005 and noise multiplier 1; its add/remove and replacement distances are 0.074991699310.07499169931 and 0.069991700350.06999170035. CPU or XPU dispatch can differ from CUDA, so only native CUDA executions count as evidence.

Appendix B Experimental Records and Provenance

Records.

Every reported number traces to a machine-readable result record that stores the experiment source digest, package-source digests, the loaded CUDA library digest, the inputs and all case traces. The plotted values in Figures 2–5 are derived from these records by a standard-library script, and the resolution estimate in §6.5 uses exact binomial tails; both scripts accompany the artifact.

Retained failures.

We report failed attempts alongside the accepted ones. The first OPT-125M reachability run rejected an incorrect 128-token shape assumption before loading the model; the accepted run uses the full 256-token windows. In the C=1C{=}1 screen, four BF16 control attempts failed their exact-adapter initialization check before measurement; a separately versioned supplement loaded the canonical FP32 adapter bytes and completed exactly those four controls, so the screen comprises 86 measured conditions and four retained rejections rather than 90 independent observations. The gradient-level mask intervention exists in an original and a corrected version, and both are retained together with the CPU validation of the accepted one.

Independent reconciliation.

All raw arrays of the 40 selected-radius native cases were reconciled on CPU in FP64, reproducing every reported distance. For the release audit, the 1,024-draw-per-side qualification runs, which reproduce both parent releases bitwise, are excluded from the reported counts. A CPU pass verified all eight shard identities, seeds, scalar hashes, shapes and the complete two-million-draw coverage.
